topics.title: Cardiac cycle and heart sounds
points: S1 is closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves and marks the start of systole.
S2 is closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves and marks the start of diastole.
Isovolumetric contraction: all valves closed, pressure rising, volume unchanged.
S3 happens in early diastole during rapid ventricular filling; can be normal in young people and pregnancy, otherwise suggests volume overload or heart failure.
S4 is atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle (for example LV hypertrophy); always abnormal in adults.

cards.front: When in the cycle do you hear S3?
cards.back: Early diastole, during rapid ventricular filling
Atrial contraction pushing blood into a stiff, noncompliant ventricle

cards.front: Phase between mitral closure and aortic opening?

questions.q: A 68-year-old with long-standing hypertension has an extra heart sound just before S1. What does it most likely reflect?
options: Rapid ventricular filling into a dilated ventricle
Atrial contraction against a stiff left ventricle
Opening of a stenotic mitral valve
questions.explanation: A sound just before S1 is S4. It comes from atrial kick against a stiff, hypertrophied LV, common with long-standing hypertension.

questions.q: During which phase are all four heart valves closed while ventricular pressure rises?
questions.explanation: In isovolumetric contraction the AV valves have closed and the semilunar valves have not opened yet, so pressure rises with no change in volume.

questions.q: An S3 is most consistent with which condition in a 60-year-old?
questions.explanation: In older adults S3 points to increased filling into a dilated, volume-overloaded ventricle, as in heart failure.

topics.title: Metabolic acidosis and the anion gap
points: Anion gap = Na minus (Cl + HCO3). Normal is roughly 8 to 12.
Winter's formula predicts respiratory compensation: expected PaCO2 = 1.5 x HCO3 + 8, plus or minus 2.
High anion gap causes include lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis, renal failure, and toxic alcohols (methanol, ethylene glycol).
Normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) causes include diarrhea and renal tubular acidosis.

cards.front: Classic GI cause of normal anion gap acidosis
Two toxic alcohols that cause high anion gap acidosis

questions.q: Na 140, Cl 104, HCO3 12. What is the anion gap?
HCO3 is 14. Using Winter's formula, what PaCO2 range shows appropriate respiratory compensation?
questions.explanation: 1.5 × 14 + 8 = 29, so 27 to 31 is expected. Higher means a concurrent respiratory acidosis.

questions.q: Which cause gives a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis?
questions.explanation: Diarrhea loses bicarbonate and chloride rises to compensate, so the gap stays normal. The others add unmeasured anions.

topics.title: Cholinergic drugs and toxicity
points: Organophosphates irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing cholinergic excess.
Organophosphate treatment: atropine for muscarinic effects plus pralidoxime to regenerate acetylcholinesterase (if given early).
Anticholinergic toxicity: hot, dry, flushed skin, dilated pupils, urinary retention, delirium.

cards.back: Irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase, so ACh builds up

questions.q: A farmer has miosis, salivation, bronchorrhea, and muscle fasciculations. Which drug reverses the fasciculations?
questions.explanation: Atropine only blocks muscarinic effects. Fasciculations are nicotinic, so pralidoxime (regenerating acetylcholinesterase) is needed.
Muscarinic blockade causes urinary retention, along with dry skin, mydriasis, and tachycardia.

topics.title: Glycolysis regulation
points: PFK-1 is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis.
PFK-1 is activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and inhibited by ATP and citrate.
Net yield of glycolysis is 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose.
Pyruvate kinase deficiency causes hemolytic anemia because RBCs depend on glycolysis for ATP.

cards.front: Net ATP from glycolysis per glucose

questions.q: Which molecule most strongly activates PFK-1 in the fed state?
questions.explanation: Insulin raises fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, the most potent activator of PFK-1. Citrate and ATP inhibit it.

questions.q: A child has chronic hemolytic anemia and an enzyme defect in glycolysis. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?
questions.explanation: Pyruvate kinase deficiency is the classic glycolytic cause of hemolysis. G6PD is in the pentose phosphate pathway, not glycolysis.
